audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding sentence is verbatim at McAllister & McAllister 1991:134 in the SIL PDF we hold (p. 21), and the Hartzler afterword caveat is verbatim at pp. 141-142. (2) Deciding source: a 1991 SIL field phonology article, the only description of Doutai in existence per Glottolog (1 descriptive ref) and the SIL archive (1 item for tds); Clouse 1997 (held) independently states stress is non-contrastive across Lakes Plain and defers to McAllister for Doutai. No reference grammar, dissertation, JIPA illustration or instrumental study was found in any bibliography opened; the language is moribund (~335 speakers in 1991). (3) list of works to obtain: empty — nothing unheld is known to exist. sources.note: Segmental survey only: consonant inventory, lenition, nasals, fricativised vowels, semivowels. Doutai facts (/g/ phoneme, [p]~[phi] variation, no nasals, 5-vowel vs 7-vowel analysis, no closed syllables) are all attributed to McAllister & McAllister 1991, the catalog's own source. No statement on Doutai word stress, accent or tone anywhere; the only tone mentions are a footnote on Fayu/Edopi minimal pairs (printed p.6 fn.7: 'Kugler and Kugler do not mark tone for the few minimal pairs, Kim and Kim list only two minimal pairs') and the conclusion's call for future tone research. sources.citation: Clouse, Duane A. 1997. Towards a reconstruction and reclassification of the Lakes Plain languages of Irian Jaya. In Karl J. Franklin (ed.), Papers in Papuan linguistics No. 2 (Pacific Linguistics A-85), 133-236. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University.
sources.note: Section 11 'Tone typology' (p.152): tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages and was most likely a feature of some protolanguages; all modern languages have at least high and low tone; Duvle and Sikaritai have only these (Martin 1991 analyses Sikaritai as pitch accent); Obokuitai has a fall; 'Doutai (McAllister 1991), Edopi (Kim 1995) and all the western Tariku languages have a fall and a rise'; four of Iau's eight tones 'correspond to the four tones found in the other Lakes Plain languages'. Secondhand for Doutai (author's fieldwork is Kirikiri); no TBU/domain/rule analysis.…
